name: Distance
seoDesc: Distance: a free math calculator that walks you through 55 values, with the formula spelled out and a worked example.
summary: The distance calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports distance immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. That makes it useful for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Distance calculator work?
sections.html:
The Distance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports distance in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type and the dimensions); then you type in the distance (Result).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • Dimensions: pick the option that matches your case — 4 options, such as 1D, 2D and 3D. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

sections.title: The formula behind the Distance calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

X₂=X₁ + the square root of ((distance ^ 2) − ((((dimensions > 3) ? ( (K₁ − K₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 1) ? ( (Y₁ − Y₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 2) ? ( (Z₁ − Z₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))))
Distance=the absolute value of (B + M × X₁ − Y₁) ÷ the square root of ((M ^ 2) + 1)
X₂=X₃ + the square root of ((distance 2-3 ^ 2) − ((((dimensions > 3) ? ( (K₂ − K₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 1) ? ( (Y₂ − Y₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) − ((((dimensions > 2) ? ( (Z₂ − Z₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))))
Distance 1-3=the square root of ((X₁ − X₃ ^ 2) + ((((dimensions > 3) ? ( (K₁ − K₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) + ((((dimensions > 1) ? ( (Y₁ − Y₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) + ((((dimensions > 2) ? ( (Z₁ − Z₃ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))))
Distance 1-2=the square root of ((X₁ − X₂ ^ 2) + ((((dimensions > 3) ? ( (K₁ − K₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) + ((((dimensions > 1) ? ( (Y₁ − Y₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))) + ((((dimensions > 2) ? ( (Z₁ − Z₂ ^ 2) ) : ( 0 )))))
Distance=the absolute value of (B − B₂) ÷ the square root of ((M ^ 2) + 1)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Type set to 2 points, Dimensions set to 2D, x₁ = 10 and y₁ = 10. The calculator returns Distance = 9.950372.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Distance = 9.950372 should be roughly the size you expected from Type set to 2 points and Dimensions set to 2D.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Distance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Distance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns distance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Distance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 18 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Distance = 9.950372. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Distance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
